---
title: "Day 21 demo: test a spectral candidate"
---

**Question:** what changes when a candidate must explain a complete set of
observations rather than only its molecular formula?

Allow **10 minutes**: predict for 2, inspect competing candidates for 5, then
write an assignment and limitation for 3. All traces are fixed **simulated
teaching data**, not measured sample spectra.

```{=html}
<section class="chem-demo" id="day21" aria-label="Simulated IR and proton-NMR candidate-testing laboratory">
<p>Enable JavaScript to compare a drawn candidate against supplied formula, IR and NMR clues.</p>
</section>
<script src="../interactives/core.js"></script>

```

## Predict

Unknown U1 is **C₄H₈O₂**. Could both an ester and a carboxylic acid fit the
formula? Which observation would make a stronger comparison than the formula
alone?

For simple first-order proton NMR here, $n$ equivalent neighbouring H give
$n+1$ lines. Integration counts relative H area; a quartet's four lines do
not mean four H. In an IR transmittance trace, absorption appears as a dip.

## Explore

1. Compare ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid using **Formula only**.
2. Add the complete IR and identify which functional-group prediction changes.
3. Use all clues. Assign the 2H quartet, 3H triplet and remaining 3H singlet
   in U1 rather than merely selecting the green outcome.
4. Try **Second unknown** and test ethanol against dimethyl ether. Then reset.

## Supplied data and worked check

U1 has carbonyl absorption without a broad O–H feature and proton signals
**1.25 ppm triplet, 3H; 2.05 ppm singlet, 3H; 4.12 ppm quartet, 2H**. Ethyl
ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, accounts for an ethyl pair and an acetyl methyl
singlet. Butanoic acid predicts acid O–H and lacks the O–CH₂/acetyl pattern.

U2 is **C₂H₆O**, with broad O–H, no carbonyl, and **1.18 ppm triplet, 3H;
3.65 ppm quartet, 2H; an exchangeable broad OH signal, 1H** in this illustrative
model. Ethanol fits; dimethyl ether has the same formula but no OH and would
not give that proton pattern.

## Model limits

Peak positions, shapes and exchange depend on conditions. The listed patterns
are introductory first-order examples, not a general spectral solver. Green
means the candidate fits the **selected supplied evidence**, not that every
possible alternative is excluded or the sample is pure. A filename is not
identity evidence. See the local [spectroscopy problem bank](../spectroscopy/exercise.qmd).
